Greyhollow is a mining town of slate roofs and smoking chimneys, cut into the side of a cold mountain where the wind never quite stops. Its people live by iron and stone, and they trust both more than they trust anything that comes out of the deep.

You are Brakka Ironvein, a hill dwarf and for six years a guard at the Temple of the Anvil Father. You know these streets and most of the faces in them. Three days ago, three miners went down into the old north workings, tunnels sealed a generation ago. None came back. Last night a fourth man staggered out of the dark alone, babbling about lights that walk, and was dead before dawn. The town council will brick up the entrance at sunrise, missing men or not. Old Prior Hessa has asked you to go down first and bring back whoever can still be brought back.

It is late afternoon. The sun is low behind the peaks and the shadows run long. You stand at the mine mouth in chain mail, shield on your arm, longsword at your hip, the temple's hooded lantern in your hand. Before you, the old timber frame leans over a black opening. The planks that once sealed it lie pulled aside, and cold air breathes out of the dark, smelling of wet stone. Something pale glints faintly on the floor a few paces in.

What does Brakka do?
I raise the hooded lantern and open the shutter a little. Then I step carefully toward the pale glint, shield up and one hand near my sword hilt, watching the floor and the walls as I go.

You ease the shutter open a hand's width. A narrow wedge of amber light slides across the rock, and you step in with your shield high.

The pale glint is a miner's pick lying on the floor, its iron head dusted white. Beside it, the dust is scuffed by boots: three sets going in, deep and hurried, and one set coming back out, shorter and stumbling, with a smear where a hand dragged along the wall. Your sharp eyes also catch something the miners' tracks overlie. A fine pale powder, like crushed chalk, lies in a thin trail down the passage. It looks as though something has passed this way, and it did not leave bootprints.

The tunnel slopes down and bends north, its timber props black with age and sweating cold water. Somewhere far ahead, very faintly, you hear a slow drip. Beneath it there is something else, a soft rhythmic tick, like a pick on stone, but too regular for any man.

Behind you the sunlight is already thinning to gold at the mouth. What does Brakka do?

I crouch and look closer at the chalk-marked pick and the pale powder trail, touching the powder carefully with a gloved finger and sniffing it. Then I pick up the pick if it seems safe, and start following the trail down the tunnel, keeping my light low and my ears tuned to that ticking.

You crouch and rub a pinch of the powder between glove and thumb. It is gritty, and finer than chalk. Held to the lantern, tiny white flecks glitter in it, and the smell is faint and dry and wrong. Ground bone, you judge, mixed with stone dust, and ground long ago, not freshly. Whatever walked here did not sweat or bleed. It shed.

The pick is sound and cold, a miner's tool with a worn ash handle, and nothing about it seems dangerous. You take it. It may tell the town's families something, if no one comes home to say it themselves.

You follow the trail with the lantern low. The tunnel descends in a long slope, props leaning, the air growing colder and still. After a short while the ticking grows clearer: tock, tock, tock, slow and patient, from somewhere ahead and to the right.

At last the passage opens on a cross-cut where two galleries meet. The left gallery is half buried by an old rockfall. The right runs on, and the powder trail bends into it. In the dust at the junction lies a boot, a man's, with the laces still tied. The ticking comes from the right gallery, near now, perhaps forty paces off. Past the bend, you can just see a faint, cold, bluish glow on the wall.

What does Brakka do?

I check the boot quickly for anything useful, then close the lantern shutter down to a thin slit so my light doesn't announce me. I move up the right gallery slowly, shield forward, to the bend and peek around it toward the bluish glow.

It is not easy. Chain mail does not creep. Each step brings a small chink of rings, and in the hush of the tunnel it sounds as loud as a dropped pan. At the bend, the ticking stops.

RULE Combat Step by Step:
1.  **Determine surprise.** The GM determines whether anyone involved in the combat encounter is surprised.
2.  **Establish positions.** The GM decides where all the characters and monsters are located. Given the adventurers' marching order or their stated positions in the room or other location, the GM figures out where the adversaries are/how far away and in what direction.
3.  **Roll initiative.** Everyone involved in the combat encounter rolls initiative, determining the order of combatants' turns.
4.  **Take turns.** Each participant in the battle takes a turn in initiative order.
5.  **Begin the next round.** When everyone involved in the combat has had a turn, the round ends. Repeat step 4 until the fighting stops.

The rules sections these steps name, in full:

RULE Surprise:
A band of adventurers sneaks up on a bandit camp, springing from the trees to attack them. A gelatinous cube glides down a dungeon passage, unnoticed by the adventurers until the cube engulfs one of them. In these situations, one side of the battle gains surprise over the other.

The GM determines who might be surprised. If neither side tries to be stealthy, they automatically notice each other. Otherwise, the GM compares the Dexterity (Stealth) checks of anyone hiding with the passive Wisdom (Perception) score of each creature on the opposing side. Any character or monster that doesn't notice a threat is surprised at the start of the encounter.

If you're surprised, you can't move or take an action on your first turn of the combat, and you can't take a reaction until that turn ends. A member of a group can be surprised even if the other members aren't.

RULE The Order of Combat:
A typical combat encounter is a clash between two sides, a flurry of weapon swings, feints, parries, footwork, and spellcasting. The game organizes the chaos of combat into a cycle of rounds and turns. A **round** represents about 6 seconds in the game world. During a round, each participant in a battle takes a **turn**. The order of turns is determined at the beginning of a combat encounter, when everyone rolls initiative. Once everyone has taken a turn, the fight continues to the next round if neither side has defeated the other.

RULE Initiative:
Initiative determines the order of turns during combat. When combat starts, every participant makes a Dexterity check to determine their place in the initiative order. The GM makes one roll for an entire group of identical creatures, so each member of the group acts at the same time.

The GM ranks the combatants in order from the one with the highest Dexterity check total to the one with the lowest. This is the order (called the initiative order) in which they act during each round. The initiative order remains the same from round to round.

If a tie occurs, the GM decides the order among tied GM-controlled creatures, and the players decide the order among their tied characters. The GM can decide the order if the tie is between a monster and a player character. Optionally, the GM can have the tied characters and monsters each roll a d20 to determine the order, highest roll going first.

You press the miner's pick into Dorrin's hands and give him your instructions. He nods, swallows, and settles behind the prop. "Anvil keep you," he whispers.

You take the stair down, step by step, shutter at a thread. The stone steps are worn hollow in the middle, cut by hands long dead, and the blue light grows with every turn. Your chain mail will not be quiet. Each step brings a soft chink of rings, and halfway down you hear the gentle bobbing and whispering of small things in the hall below fall silent all at once.

The stair opens into the Lamp Hall: a long, low chamber with pillars of living rock and a floor of smooth black stone. Along the walls, in iron brackets, burn cold blue flames with no oil or wick. Two stone slabs stand at the far end, and on them lie a woman and a grey-bearded old man, still, but breathing, their wrists chained to iron rings. Six small blue flames, each caged in a little ribcage and scuttling on bone legs, have turned toward you from among the pillars. Behind them, between you and the slabs, stands the taller figure Dorrin described: a hunched thing in a green rotted foreman's coat, with a blue lamp where its head should be. It lifts a rusted miner's hammer.

They know you are here. What does Brakka do?

I stay on the bottom steps so the stair mouth limits how many can come at me at once, shield up and lantern fully open. "Anvil Father, hold my arm," I mutter, and I wait for the first of them to come into reach so I can cut it down, with Second Wind ready if I get hurt.

RULE Combat Step by Step:
1.  **Determine surprise.** The GM determines whether anyone involved in the combat encounter is surprised.
2.  **Establish positions.** The GM decides where all the characters and monsters are located. Given the adventurers' marching order or their stated positions in the room or other location, the GM figures out where the adversaries are/how far away and in what direction.
3.  **Roll initiative.** Everyone involved in the combat encounter rolls initiative, determining the order of combatants' turns.
4.  **Take turns.** Each participant in the battle takes a turn in initiative order.
5.  **Begin the next round.** When everyone involved in the combat has had a turn, the round ends. Repeat step 4 until the fighting stops.

The rules sections these steps name, in full:

RULE Surprise:
A band of adventurers sneaks up on a bandit camp, springing from the trees to attack them. A gelatinous cube glides down a dungeon passage, unnoticed by the adventurers until the cube engulfs one of them. In these situations, one side of the battle gains surprise over the other.

The GM determines who might be surprised. If neither side tries to be stealthy, they automatically notice each other. Otherwise, the GM compares the Dexterity (Stealth) checks of anyone hiding with the passive Wisdom (Perception) score of each creature on the opposing side. Any character or monster that doesn't notice a threat is surprised at the start of the encounter.

If you're surprised, you can't move or take an action on your first turn of the combat, and you can't take a reaction until that turn ends. A member of a group can be surprised even if the other members aren't.

RULE The Order of Combat:
A typical combat encounter is a clash between two sides, a flurry of weapon swings, feints, parries, footwork, and spellcasting. The game organizes the chaos of combat into a cycle of rounds and turns. A **round** represents about 6 seconds in the game world. During a round, each participant in a battle takes a **turn**. The order of turns is determined at the beginning of a combat encounter, when everyone rolls initiative. Once everyone has taken a turn, the fight continues to the next round if neither side has defeated the other.

RULE Initiative:
Initiative determines the order of turns during combat. When combat starts, every participant makes a Dexterity check to determine their place in the initiative order. The GM makes one roll for an entire group of identical creatures, so each member of the group acts at the same time.

The GM ranks the combatants in order from the one with the highest Dexterity check total to the one with the lowest. This is the order (called the initiative order) in which they act during each round. The initiative order remains the same from round to round.

If a tie occurs, the GM decides the order among tied GM-controlled creatures, and the players decide the order among their tied characters. The GM can decide the order if the tie is between a monster and a player character. Optionally, the GM can have the tied characters and monsters each roll a d20 to determine the order, highest roll going first.

story.text:
STORY SO FAR (start of game to end of turn 15)

SETTING AND CLOCK
Game date: 12 Leaffall, year 1. The game started at 5:00 PM. Greyhollow is a mining town cut into a cold mountainside. The council will brick up the North Workings entrance at sunrise on 13 Leaffall. The temple's prior is the old dwarf Hessa (Temple of the Anvil Father, Greyhollow). The Anvil Father is a dwarven forge god.

THE PC: BRAKKA IRONVEIN (hill dwarf fighter 1, acolyte)
Brakka was a temple guard for six years. Hessa sent him with a borrowed hooded lantern to find the missing miners. He had chain mail, shield, longsword (Dueling), light crossbow, 15 gp, and 10 rations and torches. He had no dagger.

EVENTS, IN ORDER
1. Brakka found a miner's pick with a chalk-white head just inside the entrance. Three sets of boots went in and one came out. A trail of fine ground-bone-and-stone powder ran down the tunnel, with no bootprints.
2. He picked up the pick. The tunnel sloped down and bent north to a cross-cut. The left gallery is buried by a rockfall, and a laced boot lay at the junction. The right gallery leads to a chamber lit by cold blue veins in the rock.
3. His Stealth in chain mail failed, so two skeletons in rotted miners' leathers noticed him. Brakka fought them at the gallery mouth. He took 6, then 6, then 3 damage and used Second Wind (healed 3). He killed both with his longsword, ending at 2 HP, and earned 100 XP.
4. He freed the bound miner, Dorrin Pell, a lean sandy-haired man of about thirty. Dorrin said that he, Tamsin Vey and old Orrick broke into a sealed hall and were herded by "walking lights", small blue flames in bone cages on bone legs. He described six or seven of them, plus a taller thing in a rotted green foreman's coat with a blue lamp for a head, which gives the orders. Dorrin was left tied up as a spare. Tamsin and Orrick were taken down a stair at the back of the chamber to the Lamp Hall, where they lie chained on stone slabs, alive when last seen (the day before, 11 Leaffall).
5. Brakka took a one-hour short rest (to 6:23 PM), spent a hit die for 11 HP, and regained Second Wind. He left Dorrin behind a wedged prop in the gallery and gave him the miner's pick. His instruction to Dorrin: if Brakka isn't back by sundown, crawl out and tell Prior Hessa what's below.
6. Brakka went down the stair (about 6:27 PM) and failed Stealth again. In the Lamp Hall the foreman raised a rusted miner's hammer, and three flame-cages attacked.
7. The fight was ruled as: Flame-cages = Skeleton stat block (13 HP, AC 13, +4 to hit, 1d6+2); Lamp Foreman = Zombie stat block (22 HP, AC 8, Slam +3, 1d6+1, Undead Fortitude). Brakka held the stair mouth, so only one enemy could reach him at a time.
8. Brakka killed Flame-cage 2. Flame-cage 1 (6 of 13 HP left) hit him down to 1 HP, then to 0 HP after he used Second Wind (healed 3). Death saves were one success and one failure, then a critical hit (2 failures). Brakka Ironvein died at about 6:28 PM.
9. One flame-cage was destroyed. One flame-cage is wounded, and the Lamp Foreman is untouched at 22 HP. A third flame-cage and further lights are unaccounted for. I narrated that the other small lights bobbed behind the pillars, waiting, but only three came at the stair.

STATE AT END OF TURN 15 / AFTER DEATH
- Brakka's body, shield and longsword lie at the foot of the stair.
- Dorrin waits above with the pick.
- Tamsin Vey and Orrick are chained on slabs in the Lamp Hall.
- Time is Day 1, 6:28 PM, 12 Leaffall.
- The fight was ended with end_fight.
- XP 100 was earned.

NEW CHARACTER IN PROGRESS
The player wants a new fighter, someone from Greyhollow who heard Hessa's call after Brakka didn't return. The clock continues. I used new_pc with roll_scores, and the scores rolled are 15, 14, 13, 13, 11 and 10. I asked the player to assign them and to choose race, fighting style, two skills, gear, name and short background. Nothing is confirmed yet. Next steps: build the sheet with new_pc (no confirm first), show it, get a yes, then call again with confirm and an opening paragraph. The new PC starts at level 1.

DM DECISIONS NOT YET REVEALED
- The walking lights are animated by the blue-veined rock and the foreman-thing in the Lamp Hall. They are not yet explained further. I planned a cause linked to the sealed workings, which I haven't decided.
- The foreman and the flame-cage remain in the Lamp Hall, and the rest of the lights are somewhere nearby. The new PC will need a way past them, perhaps with Dorrin's help or the pick.
- The sealing-up deadline at sunrise still applies.

NOTEBOOK ENTRIES CREATED
Brakka Ironvein, Greyhollow, Temple of the Anvil Father, Prior Hessa, North Workings, Missing miners (quest, open), Chalk-marked pick, Bone miners, Anvil Father, Bound miner (Dorrin Pell), Tamsin Vey, Orrick, Lamp Hall (inside North Workings), Death of Brakka Ironvein. Lamp Foreman and Flame-cage have not yet been given entries and should be added.
